Custom
kŭs´tum
n. (a toll or duty; also habitual practice; rendering Greek telos and ethos)
From Latin consuetudo, habit — and by extension the customary duty levied on goods. The KJV uses both senses.

Biblical Definition

Custom means both a levied duty and an established habit. Matthew is called from the receipt of custom (Mat 9:9), and Paul commands that dues be paid: “Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom” (Rom 13:7). The other sense governs Christ's own practice: “he came to Nazareth… and, as his custom was, he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day” (Luk 4:16). Hebrews warns against forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, “as the manner of some is” (Heb 10:25).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines custom as frequent or common use, habitual practice; and as tribute, toll or tax, the duties imposed on goods.

expand to see more

CUSTOM, n. Frequent or common use, or practice; a frequent repetition of the same act; habitual practice.

2. A buying of goods; practice of frequenting a shop and purchasing.

3. Tribute, toll or tax; that is, cost or charge paid to the public.

Key Scripture

Mat 9:9 — "And as Jesus passed forth from thence, he saw a man, named Matthew, sitting at the receipt of custom: and he saith unto him, Follow me. And he arose, and followed him."

Rom 13:7 — "Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour."

Luk 4:16 — "And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up: and, as his custom was, he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day, and stood up for to read."

Heb 10:25 — "Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching."

Modern Corruption

Habit is dismissed as dead routine by people whose devotion collapses without it — while Luke records that gathered worship was Christ's own settled custom.

expand to see more

Luke 4:16 contains four words that answer a long modern argument: as his custom was. The Son of God, who needed no instruction and had nothing to learn from the reader in the Nazareth synagogue, attended weekly by habit. The passage is not about the quality of that synagogue — the congregation tried to kill Him before the day was out. It is about a practice maintained regardless, which is what a custom is.

Romans 13:7 keeps the other sense from being spiritualized away. Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour. Paying customs duties honestly is placed in the same sentence as honour and fear, which means a believer's tax return belongs to his discipleship and not merely to his accounting.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek telos (G5056), a toll or custom duty; telonion (G5058), the tax booth; ethos (G1485), a habit or established usage.

expand to see more

Greek telos (G5056) — custom, toll; Matthew 17:25, Romans 13:7.

Greek telonion (G5058) — the receipt of custom, tax booth; Matthew 9:9, Mark 2:14.

Greek ethos (G1485) — custom, habit; Luke 4:16, 22:39, as he was wont, to the mount of Olives.

Usage

"“Sitting at the receipt of custom” — where Matthew was called."

"“Custom to whom custom” — duties paid as discipleship."

"“As his custom was, he went into the synagogue” — habit that needed no inspiration."
